description: Silent cinema, the talkies, post-war cinema boom, TV from the 1950s and the streaming age.
content_html:
The Arrival of Cinema

Moving pictures reached British audiences at the end of the nineteenth century. The Lumière brothers demonstrated their Cinématographe in London in February 1896, and purpose-built cinemas began to appear in British towns and cities from around 1907. Early silent films were short, simple and accompanied by a piano or organ played live in the cinema. By the early 1920s, cinema had become the most popular form of mass entertainment in Britain, particularly for working-class urban audiences.

The 1920s saw the construction of purpose-built “picture palaces” — large, ornate cinemas designed to offer audiences a glamorous escape from everyday life. By the mid-1930s, the United Kingdom had around 4,300 cinemas with a combined weekly attendance of approximately 18-20 million. Going to the pictures was a regular weekly habit for millions of British people, particularly for young adults and courting couples.

Key Fact

The talkies arrived when the American film The Jazz Singer was released in 1927, featuring synchronised speech and song. British cinemas quickly converted to sound equipment, and audiences grew even larger. The 1930s were the golden age of British cinema attendance.

British Cinema in the 1930s and 1940s

Hollywood dominated, but British cinema had its own identity. Ealing Studios produced a distinctive strand of British comedy and drama from the late 1930s onwards, culminating in the classic Ealing comedies of the late 1940s and early 1950s — films such as Passport to Pimlico (1949), Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949), and The Lavender Hill Mob (1951). These films reflected British culture, humour and social anxieties in ways that American films could not.

Cinema attendance peaked in Britain in 1946 at approximately 1.64 billion tickets sold in a single year — equivalent to an average of about 31 visits per person per year. This figure illustrates how central cinema had become to British social life in the immediate post-war period. The cinema was warm, cheap, and offered two hours of escapism from the austerity of post-war Britain.

The BBC launched the world’s first regular public television service from Alexandra Palace in November 1936. The service was suspended during the Second World War and resumed in June 1946. Television ownership grew slowly at first because sets were expensive. The 1953 coronation of Queen Elizabeth II was the decisive moment that drove mass television adoption: an estimated 20 million people watched it in Britain, most on sets owned by neighbours or in public venues.

ITV (Independent Television) launched in September 1955, breaking the BBC’s monopoly and introducing commercial broadcasting. Competition improved programming quality and drove up television ownership. Colour television was introduced on BBC2 in 1967 and on BBC1 and ITV in 1969. By 1971, colour licences outnumbered black-and-white ones for the first time.

Cinema’s Decline and Television’s Dominance

The relationship between cinema and television was initially competitive, and cinema lost. British cinema admissions fell from 1.64 billion in 1946 to around 501 million in 1960, and to approximately 194 million by 1970. Hundreds of cinemas closed; many were converted into bingo halls. Television, free at the point of use (after the initial set cost and licence fee), available at home and increasingly offering a wide range of content, was simply more convenient.

Cinema survived by differentiating itself: large screens, better sound, and ultimately blockbuster films that could not be replicated at home. The invention of the VCR (video cassette recorder) in the late 1970s and its mass adoption in the 1980s seemed to threaten cinemas further, but in fact the two co-existed as the appetite for screen entertainment grew. Cinema admissions have broadly recovered since the 1990s, driven by multiplex development, blockbuster franchises and digital presentation.

The late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries brought further transformation. Digital recording, the DVD, and then broadband internet changed how people consumed screen entertainment again. Streaming services such as Netflix (available in the UK from 2012) and later Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video changed viewing habits fundamentally. By the early 2020s, streaming had overtaken traditional broadcast television as the primary way many younger viewers consumed screen entertainment.

The shift to on-demand, personalised viewing represents a significant break with the shared experience that had defined cinema and television from the 1920s to the 1990s. Instead of a nation watching the same programme at the same time, audiences fragmented into millions of individual choices. The social experience of “going to the pictures” or gathering round the television for a shared broadcast became rarer, though blockbuster cinema events retained their communal appeal.

Key Fact

The 1953 coronation of Queen Elizabeth II was watched by approximately 20 million people in Britain and was the decisive moment that drove mass adoption of television. Cinema admissions had already peaked in 1946 at around 1.64 billion, and the rise of television accelerated their rapid decline through the 1950s and 1960s.
exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Change’ question on screen entertainment, show that you understand the direction of change and what drove it — not just that television replaced cinema, but why: convenience, cost, the licence-fee model, the 1953 coronation. For source utility questions, remember to judge how useful a source is for a specific enquiry by combining its content, provenance and your own contextual knowledge — a film poster from the 1930s is useful for what cinema advertised to audiences but less useful for understanding audience experience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cinema arrived in Britain in 1896; the talkies (1927) and purpose-built picture palaces drove attendance to a peak of approximately 1.64 billion admissions in 1946.
  • The BBC launched TV in 1936 (resuming 1946); the 1953 coronation drove mass ownership; ITV launched 1955; colour TV 1967–1969. Television had largely replaced cinema as Britain’s dominant screen entertainment by the 1960s.
  • Digital technology and streaming (Netflix in UK from 2012) shifted screen consumption from shared broadcast events to individual on-demand viewing, continuing the pattern of personalisation that began with the VCR.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of early British cinema in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. purpose-built picture palaces were constructed in the 1920s offering a glamorous escape / silent films were accompanied by live piano or organ music / cinema became the most popular form of mass entertainment for urban working-class audiences. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the development of television in Britain between 1936 and 1970.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. the BBC launched the world's first regular public television service in November 1936 (feature + detail); colour television was introduced on BBC2 in 1967, with BBC1 and ITV following in 1969, transforming the viewing experience (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why cinema attendance fell sharply in Britain during the 1950s and 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed causal explanation linking rising television ownership (driven by the 1953 coronation and ITV launch in 1955), the convenience of home viewing, and the licence-fee model making television effectively free at the point of use. Specific evidence. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the introduction of ITV in 1955 for British television audiences.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. competition broke the BBC’s monopoly, improved programming quality, drove faster television adoption, introduced advertising-funded content distinct from the licence-fee model. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the introduction of talking pictures in 1927 for the development of British cinema?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (rapid conversion of cinemas to sound equipment, audience growth, transformation of the film industry) AND over time (sound became the new baseline; silent film never returned; Hollywood dominance grew). Uses evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Television was the single most important development in British entertainment in the twentieth century.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from the period 1896 to the present in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing television against cinema, streaming, radio and music. Agrees with evidence (mass adoption, 1953 coronation, replacing cinema dominance, fragmented viewing). Challenges by noting cinema's peak was pre-television; streaming represents a further transformation; radio was also transformative (see 1920s). Traces the full modern period. Overall conclusion. Secure: Addresses both sides with evidence. Developing: Limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: In which year did the BBC launch the world's first regular public television service?
What event in 1953 drove mass adoption of television sets across Britain?
options: The coronation of Queen Elizabeth II

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ arrived with The Jazz Singer in 1927, replacing silent films and transforming British cinema.
ITV, Britain's first commercial broadcaster funded by advertising, launched in _____.
Match each date or term to its significance in screen entertainment:
right: Peak year for British cinema admissions at approximately 1.64 billion
Year colour television was introduced on BBC2
On-demand internet video delivery that transformed viewing from the 2010s

flashcard_questions.a: Films without synchronised sound, relying on visual performance and live musical accompaniment.

flashcard_questions.q: When did talkies arrive in Britain, and what was the landmark film?
flashcard_questions.a: 1927; The Jazz Singer, the first feature with synchronised speech and song.

When did the BBC launch the world's first regular public television service?

flashcard_questions.a: The coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.

flashcard_questions.a: 1955, funded by advertising rather than a licence fee.

flashcard_questions.a: A home video recording and playback system, widely adopted from the early 1980s.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Netflix become available in the UK?

flashcard_questions.a: Delivering video via the internet for immediate consumption without downloading a permanent file.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one Ealing comedy produced in the late 1940s or early 1950s.
flashcard_questions.a: Passport to Pimlico (1949), Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949), or The Lavender Hill Mob (1951).

glossary_terms.definition: Films produced without synchronised sound, relying on visual performance, intertitles and live musical accompaniment.
Films with synchronised sound, which replaced silent films from 1927 onwards, transforming the cinema industry.
Britain's first commercial television broadcaster, launched in 1955 and funded by advertising rather than a licence fee.
A home video recording and playback system, widely adopted from the early 1980s, that allowed viewers to watch recorded films at home.
A method of delivering video and audio content via the internet for immediate consumption, without downloading a permanent file.
